question: What is @PathVariable in Spring MVC?
title: @PathVariable in Spring MVC — Extracting URL Path Segments
direct_answer: **`@PathVariable`** extracts a value from a URL path template variable. In `@GetMapping("/users/{id}")`, the `{id}` part is extracted from the actual URL and bound to the annotated parameter. Used for resource identification in REST APIs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core REST URL parameter extraction knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for resource ID instead of @PathVariable — breaks REST conventions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain REST URL convention: path variables for identity, query params for filtering

sections.title: @PathVariable Usage
@PathVariable Details
sections.content:
- **Syntax**: `{variableName}` in URL template, `@PathVariable Type variableName` in parameter
- **Name matching**: Parameter name must match template variable name OR use `@PathVariable("name")`
- **Type conversion**: Spring automatically converts String segment to `Long`, `Integer`, `UUID`, etc.
- **Multiple**: Multiple `{vars}` in URL → multiple @PathVariable params
- **Optional**: `@PathVariable(required=false)` with `Optional<T>` for optional path variables
- **REST convention**: Use PathVariable for resource identity (`/users/{id}`, `/orders/{orderId}`)
- **vs. @RequestParam**: PathVariable from URL path; RequestParam from `?key=value` query string
- **Regex**: `@GetMapping("/users/{id:[0-9]+}")` — constrain path variable to numeric only

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @PathVariable extracts a value embedded in the URL path itself. You define a template in the @GetMapping URL with curly braces — like /users/{id} — and Spring takes whatever is at that position in the actual request URL and injects it into the annotated parameter. Spring also handles type conversion automatically, so if your parameter is Long, Spring converts the String segment to a Long for you. The REST convention is to use path variables for resource identity — the ID that uniquely identifies which resource you're operating on. Query parameters are for optional filtering and pagination. So /users/42 is cleaner than /users?id=42 in REST style.

question: What is @RequestParam in Spring MVC and when do you use it?
title: @RequestParam in Spring MVC — Query String Parameter Binding
direct_answer: **`@RequestParam`** extracts parameters from the URL query string (after `?`). Example: `/users?status=ACTIVE&page=0`. Use it for optional filters, pagination, and search parameters. Supports `required=false` and `defaultValue` for optional params.

interviewer_intent.testing: Query string parameter binding — used in every list/search endpoint
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making all params required without defaultValue — breaks client code when params are omitted
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show pagination example with required=false and defaultValue

sections.title: @RequestParam Usage
@RequestParam Details
sections.content:
- **Required by default**: Missing required param → 400 Bad Request
- **`required=false`**: Make param optional — Spring injects `null` if missing
- **`defaultValue`**: Sets a default when param is absent; implicitly makes it optional
- **Type conversion**: Spring converts String to `int`, `Long`, `Boolean`, etc.
- **`@RequestParam Map<String, String>`**: Capture all query params as a map
- **List binding**: `@RequestParam List<String> ids` for repeated params: `?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3`
- **Form data**: `@RequestParam` also works for `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body (HTML form submissions)
- **Use for**: Filtering, sorting, pagination, search — optional aspects of the request

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RequestParam binds query string parameters to method parameters. These are the key-value pairs after the question mark in the URL. It's the right choice for filters, pagination parameters, and search terms — things that are optional additions to a request. By default params are required and Spring returns 400 if they're missing. Use required=false to make them optional, or provide a defaultValue which also makes them optional implicitly. A common pattern is pagination: page and size params with sensible defaults like 0 and 10. @RequestParam also works for HTML form submissions, not just JSON APIs. The big difference from @PathVariable is that path variables are for identity — which specific resource — and query params are for how you want to retrieve it.

question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam?
title: @PathVariable vs @RequestParam — URL Path vs Query String
direct_answer: **`@PathVariable`** extracts values from the **URL path** (e.g., `/users/42` where `42` is the ID). **`@RequestParam`** extracts values from the **query string** (e.g., `/users?status=ACTIVE`). PathVariable is for resource identity; RequestParam is for optional filters/options.

interviewer_intent.testing: Common interview comparison — shows REST design understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @RequestParam for IDs that should be @PathVariable — not RESTful
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the REST design rule: path for nouns/identity, query for adjectives/filtering

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
When to Use Each
sections.content:
| Aspect | @PathVariable | @RequestParam |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| Location | URL path `/users/{id}` | Query string `/users?id=1` |
| Purpose | Resource identity | Filtering, pagination, options |
| Optional | Unusual | Common (required=false) |
| Required | Usually yes | Often no |
| REST style | `/users/42` ✓ | `/users?id=42` ✗ (for identity) |
| Multiple | Nested resources | Multiple filter params |

**Rule**: If you're identifying WHICH resource, use @PathVariable. If you're describing HOW to retrieve it, use @RequestParam.

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The simple rule is: @PathVariable is for identity, @RequestParam is for options. When you want to identify a specific resource — user 42, order 7 — that goes in the path: /users/42/orders/7. When you want to filter or control how you retrieve resources — give me active users, page 2, sorted by name — those go in the query string as @RequestParam values. This follows REST design principles: the path identifies the resource hierarchy, and query parameters refine the operation. So /users/42 means 'get me user 42 specifically', while /users?status=ACTIVE means 'get me all users that are active'. Mixing these up — like /users?id=42 for a single user — works but is not considered clean REST design.

question: How do you make @RequestParam optional with a default value?
title: Optional @RequestParam with defaultValue in Spring MVC
direct_answer: Set **`required=false`** to make a `@RequestParam` optional (Spring injects `null` if missing). Set **`defaultValue="value"`** to provide a fallback value when the parameter is absent — this also implicitly makes the parameter optional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge for building flexible API endpoints
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Required params without defaults — clients must always provide all params or get 400 errors
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the pagination pattern as a concrete example of defaultValue in practice

sections.title: Optional Params and Defaults
Optional Param Options
sections.content:
- **`required=false`**: Parameter is optional; `null` injected if absent; use `Integer` not `int` (int can't be null)
- **`defaultValue`**: String value used when param absent; automatically makes param optional; parsed to the parameter type
- **`defaultValue` vs `required=false`**: `defaultValue` gives a fallback; `required=false` gives null
- **`Optional<String>` parameter type**: Java Optional also works — `Optional.empty()` when absent
- **Primitive types**: `int`, `boolean` etc. can't be null — use `Integer`, `Boolean` with `required=false`, or provide `defaultValue`
- **Best practice for pagination**: Always provide defaults (`page=0`, `size=20`) — never make clients required to send these
- **Max size guard**: Consider validating `@Max(100)` on `size` to prevent `?size=999999` attacks

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: To make a @RequestParam optional, you have two approaches. First, set required=false — Spring injects null if the parameter is missing from the URL. For primitive types like int, you'd need to use the wrapper Integer since primitives can't be null. Second, provide a defaultValue — Spring uses that string value when the parameter is absent and parses it to the parameter type. The defaultValue approach is cleaner for pagination: defaultValue='0' for page and defaultValue='20' for size means clients can omit them and get sensible defaults. Both approaches effectively make the parameter optional — the difference is whether you get null or a default value when it's missing.

question: How do you design RESTful URLs with path variables?
title: RESTful URL Design with Path Variables — Best Practices
direct_answer: RESTful URLs use **nouns** (not verbs), **hierarchical path variables** for resource identity, and **HTTP methods** for actions. Example: `GET /users/{id}`, `POST /users`, `DELETE /users/{id}/orders/{orderId}`. The path variables identify which resource; the HTTP method defines the action.

interviewer_intent.testing: REST URL design knowledge — shows thinking beyond just annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbs in URLs (/getUser, /deleteOrder) — REST uses HTTP methods for actions, not URL verbs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the full CRUD URL design for a resource with proper methods

sections.title: RESTful URL Patterns
sections.content:
```
# CRUD for users:
GET    /api/users           → list all users
POST   /api/users           → create new user
GET    /api/users/{id}      → get user by ID
PUT    /api/users/{id}      → full update user
PATCH  /api/users/{id}      → partial update user
DELETE /api/users/{id}      → delete user

# Nested resource:
GET    /api/users/{userId}/orders           → user's orders
GET    /api/users/{userId}/orders/{orderId} → specific order
POST   /api/users/{userId}/orders           → create order for user
```

sections.title: URL Design Rules
sections.content:
- **Nouns, not verbs**: `/users` not `/getUsers`; `/users/{id}` not `/deleteUser/{id}`
- **HTTP method = action**: GET = read, POST = create, PUT/PATCH = update, DELETE = delete
- **Plural nouns**: `/users` (plural) not `/user`
- **Lowercase and hyphenated**: `/api/user-profiles` not `/api/userProfiles`
- **Hierarchical nesting**: `/users/{id}/orders` for sub-resources (but keep nesting shallow)
- **No deep nesting**: `/users/{uId}/orders/{oId}/items/{iId}/details` is too deep
- **Query params for filtering**: `/users?status=ACTIVE&role=ADMIN` not `/activeAdminUsers`
- **Versioning**: `/api/v1/users` — version in path or header
- **Consistent casing**: Stick to one style throughout the API

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: RESTful URL design follows a few key principles. Use nouns, not verbs — the URL identifies a resource, not an action. So /users not /getUsers, /users/42 not /getUserById/42. The HTTP method tells you what action to take: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE deletes. Use plural nouns for collections: /users not /user. For nested resources like a user's orders, use hierarchical paths: /users/42/orders. Query parameters are for filtering and pagination — /users?status=active&page=0 — not for identifying the resource. Try to keep nesting to two levels maximum — if you go deeper, consider whether you really need the full hierarchy or can access the child resource directly.

question: What is @RequestParam with a List type in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestParam List — Multi-Value Query Parameters in Spring
direct_answer: Declaring `@RequestParam List<String> ids` allows clients to pass multiple values for the same parameter: `/items?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3`. Spring automatically binds all `ids` values into the List. Also supports comma-separated format with `@RequestParam("ids") String[] ids`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of multi-value query parameter binding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing @RequestParam can bind to List — trying to manually parse a comma-separated string
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both repeated param style (?ids=1&ids=2) and comma-separated style (?ids=1,2,3)

sections.title: Multi-Value @RequestParam
List @RequestParam Details
sections.content:
- **Repeated params**: `?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3` → `@RequestParam List<Long> ids` → `[1, 2, 3]`
- **`String[]`**: Works too — `@RequestParam String[] ids`
- **`List<Long>`**: Spring handles type conversion for each element
- **`required=false`**: Returns empty list `[]` by default when param absent (add `defaultValue` if needed)
- **Comma-separated**: Spring 5+ auto-splits `?tags=java,spring` into a list if using `List<String>`
- **`@RequestParam MultiValueMap`**: Get all params including multi-value params as a map
- **Use case**: Batch lookups (`?ids=1&ids=2`), multi-select filters (`?status=ACTIVE&status=PENDING`)
- **Limit client input**: Validate list size to prevent very long lists from being passed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You can bind multiple query parameter values with the same name to a List by declaring @RequestParam with a List type. If a client sends ?ids=1&ids=2&ids=3, Spring collects all the values for that parameter name into the List automatically. This is really useful for batch operations — like fetching multiple items by ID in a single request. Spring also handles type conversion for each element, so @RequestParam List<Long> works if the values are all numeric. For multi-select filters — where the user can filter by multiple statuses — you'd do the same: declare @RequestParam List<String> statuses and the client passes ?status=ACTIVE&status=PENDING.
